strengths: Comprehensive empirical analysis with systematic ablation studies across multiple procedural generation parameters (object density, types, materials, lighting, baseline randomization), providing actionable insights for practitioners
Practical computational optimizations that reduce generation time from 50.85 to 13 minutes per scene without severely degrading downstream stereo matching performance

Competitive zero-shot stereo matching results across multiple benchmarks (Middlebury 2014, ETH3D, KITTI, Booster), with Infingen-Stereo-150k achieving 4.48 on Middlebury 2014 comparable to RAFT-Stereo (8.66)
Clear practical findings about dataset design (e.g., indoor floating object scenes outperform nature scenes; mixed dataset types are most effective), useful for future synthetic dataset work

High-quality visual demonstrations of procedurally-generated scenes with good diversity (Figures 3, 8-10) and thorough ground truth annotations (camera intrinsics/extrinsics, depth maps, occlusion masks)
Promise of open-source procedural generator and released dataset (152,890 stereo pairs) that will provide community value for stereo matching research
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution is empirical parameter exploration of existing tools (Infingen, Blender) rather than novel methods for synthetic data generation; lacks algorithmic or conceptual innovation expected at top venues

Marginal performance improvements with no statistical significance testing: improvements are often within 0.1-0.5 pixels (e.g., DLNR-Infingen 2.50 vs DLNR-Mixed 2.50 on ETH3D; RAFT-Infingen 4.48 vs RAFT-Stereo 4.4); without confidence intervals, these may reflect noise

Evaluation restricted to older benchmarks (Middlebury 2014, KITTI 2012/2015, ETH3D 2018): no evaluation on recent large-scale stereo benchmarks, limiting assessment of current relevance and generalization to modern datasets

Insufficient mechanistic justification for design choices: ablation study uses only 5,000-pair subsets rather than full dataset (150k pairs), and lacks explanation of why certain parameters improve zero-shot generalization (e.g., why indoor > nature scenes)

Incomplete comparisons with alternative approaches: limited comparison with other synthetic stereo datasets (FlyingThings3D, SceneFlow, etc.) and no comparison with recent data generation methods (GAN-based, diffusion-based); Table 4 comparisons are not exhaustive
High computational cost despite optimizations (70.5 days CPU + 120 days GPU): no systematic cost comparison with competing synthetic dataset generation methods, making practical viability unclear

Limited failure mode analysis and domain gap investigation: paper acknowledges domain gap issues but provides minimal empirical analysis of remaining challenges, error types, or object categories where methods fail
Reproducibility constraints: code and dataset promised but not provided; immense parameter space makes extending or replicating work without released tools extremely difficult
No evaluation of fine-tuning or transfer learning: all results are zero-shot; fine-tuning experiments on real data (FlyingThings3D, KITTI) would strengthen claims about dataset utility

Well-documented generation process with implementation details, computational cost analysis, and promised open-source release supporting reproducibility

Weak mechanistic understanding of design choices: shows WHAT works but not WHY; finding that 'all scene types mixed' performs best undermines claims about individual design factors; lacks analysis of diversity versus quantity trade-offs

Incomplete comparisons: baselines in Table 3 are not designed for zero-shot scenarios; missing comparisons with recent domain randomization, synthetic-to-real transfer, and concurrent procedural generation methods

Well-designed dataset incorporating three diverse scene types with carefully optimized parameters for generating large-scale training data

Well-designed experiments with proper train/test protocols, standard metrics, and transparent reporting enabling reproducibility
Useful dataset and open-source procedural generator contribution to the community, achieving competitive zero-shot performance (2.50 EPE ETH3D) while enabling further research
Addresses practical computational concerns and provides guidance on generation cost optimization with tools to reduce training time
Clear presentation with effective visualizations of dataset design space and qualitative results
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—core contribution is empirical analysis combining existing tools (Blender, Infinigreen) rather than methodological innovation in procedural generation

strengths: Comprehensive systematic ablation study across multiple procedural generation parameters (floating object density/type, background objects, materials, lighting) with sound experimental methodology

Broad empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks (Middlebury, ETH3D, KITTI, Booster) and diverse stereo matching architectures (RAFT-Stereo, DLNR, IGGEV variants) demonstrating generalization of findings
Practical contributions including open-source procedural generation code and large-scale WMGStereo-150k dataset (163,666 stereo pairs) with diverse scene configurations
Clear communication of design choices and their empirical effects with effective visualizations (Figures 1, 3) showing which parameters impact performance
Thoughtful analysis of computational costs with attempted optimizations (solver tricks, render denoising) and detailed breakdown of generation expenses
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty - paper is essentially a systematic parameter search over existing Infinigen/Blender tools without proposing new scene generation methods, rendering techniques, or augmentation strategies

Performance significantly underperforms state-of-the-art: WMGStereo-150k models show 2-3× larger errors than FoundationStereo on multiple benchmarks (Middlebury 2014(H): 3.76 vs 1.10; Booster: 9.09 vs 4.16), contradicting claims of 'competitive performance'

Insights from ablations are mostly confirmatory rather than novel - that floating objects, scene realism, and avoiding transparent materials help is intuitive; lacks deep investigation into mechanisms and theoretical understanding of why findings hold

Parameter study uses only 5,000 stereo pairs per configuration while final dataset is 33× larger (163K pairs), risking conclusions that don't scale; additionally, no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported for performance differences

Prohibitively high computational costs severely limit reproducibility: 70.5 days CPU + 120 GPU days per dataset generation; total of 275 CPU + 900 GPU days without optimizations; provided optimizations only partially address this barrier

Unfair experimental comparisons conflating dataset size with design quality - while Table 3 attempts dataset normalization, the analysis remains limited and cannot isolate effects of design choices from scale effects

Limited theoretical analysis of key findings - e.g., why certain object types help differentially across benchmarks, what visual statistics correlate with performance, what features are learned from different configurations

Arbitrary design choices underspecified and unjustified - material combinations, mixing ratios in 'mixed' datasets (Table 3), parameter study sample sizes, and manual post-processing thresholds lack clear rationale

Zero-shot generalization claims somewhat misleading - significant performance degradation persists from synthetic to real data (Middlebury 2021: 6.72 error vs SceneFlow: 5.10), and evaluation is limited to mostly indoor real datasets matching synthetic data domain

Key results relegated to appendix (Table 7, Figures 6-9) and overclaiming in abstract ('best settings') when FoundationStereo achieves superior performance; paper lacks conciseness in places and misses deeper per-benchmark performance pattern analysis

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic empirical study of dataset design factors for zero-shot stereo matching, addressing a genuine practical problem through rigorous investigation across multiple benchmarks and architectures
Strong experimental validation across diverse benchmarks (Middlebury, ETH3D, KITTI, Booster) and multiple stereo models demonstrates generalizability and robustness of findings
Significant community resource contribution: WMGStereo-150k dataset (165,666 stereo pairs) and open-source procedural generation tools built on Infinigen enable reproducibility and future research

Actionable practical insights: clear finding that combining realistic indoor scenes with floating objects is most effective for zero-shot generalization provides concrete guidance for future dataset design
Computational optimization analysis demonstrating practical feasibility (reducing generation time from 275+ days to ~70 days through solver and rendering optimizations)
Well-executed experimental methodology with consistent training schedules, fixed random seeds, and multi-resolution comparisons strengthening empirical validation
Effective clear presentation with informative visualizations (Figures 1-4) and detailed documentation in appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic and methodological novelty: purely empirical study of existing dataset design choices without proposing new stereo matching methods, training paradigms, or theoretical frameworks

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: identifies WHAT works empirically but lacks explanation of WHY floating objects help zero-shot generalization or what underlying principles enable transfer from synthetic to real scenes
Modest performance improvements: WMGStereo-150k underperforms FoundationStereo on ETH3D (2.50 vs 2.13 EPE) and shows marginal improvements over natural data baselines, limiting practical advantage

Weak statistical rigor: parameter studies use only 5000 stereo pairs per setting, no error bars/confidence intervals provided, single-run results without multiple seeds make it impossible to assess statistical significance of reported differences
Incomplete failure case analysis: systematic failure modes not thoroughly investigated; problematic object types mentioned but not analyzed; limited discussion of which scenes remain challenging

Limited domain generalization analysis: primarily focuses on indoor scenes, findings may not transfer to outdoor driving, aerial, or other domains; single-domain optimization may not reflect multi-domain requirements

Insufficient baseline comparisons: missing domain adaptation methods for stereo, semi-synthetic approaches, and recent synthetic dataset design principles; dataset size not controlled when comparing with FoundationStereo

Parameter selection lacks justification: arbitrary choices (e.g., specific floating object ranges, material combinations) not well motivated; limited analysis of parameter interactions and interdependencies
Computational cost and accessibility issues: 70+ days generation time limits reproducibility for smaller institutions; no comparative efficiency analysis with alternative generation methods

Presentation limitations: dense tables (1, 7) better suited as visualizations; metric choice (EPE) not justified; application-specific metrics (occlusion, matched regions) and error analysis for challenging scenarios missing
